1H (Number Theory)

Words: 243 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 243
1H OurBigBook.com
Use the usual positive-definite convention for binary quadratic forms with negative discriminant. Reduction by integral changes of variables of determinant one produces a form ax2+bxy+cy2 with ∣b∣≤a≤c, and with b≥0 on the boundary. For completeness, replacing x by x+ny makes ∣b∣≤a; if then c<a, interchange the variables, reversing one sign to keep determinant one. The new positive leading coefficient is smaller. Repeating terminates and gives a reduced form.
For discriminant −7, 4ac−b2=7 and the reduction inequalities give 3a2≤7. Thus a=1, b is odd and ∣b∣≤1, and c=2. The boundary convention chooses b=1. Hence there is exactly one positive-definite equivalence class, represented by x2+xy+2y2.
For an odd prime p=7 represented by this form, the identity 4p=(2x+y)2+7y2 shows that −7 is a square modulo p. Here p∤y, because otherwise p∣x and p2 would divide the represented number. Conversely, if −7 is a square modulo p, choose odd b with b2≡−7(modp). Then (p,b,(b2+7)/(4p)) is an integral positive-definite form of discriminant −7. By the preceding reduction it is equivalent to the given form, so its value p at (1,0) is represented by that form. Quadratic reciprocity gives (−7/p)=(p/7), whose value is one precisely for p≡1,2,4(mod7). The exceptional primes are represented: 2=Q(0,1) and 7=Q(1,−2). Therefore
p is represented⟺p=7 or p≡1,2,4(mod7).​
(1)
Without the positive-definite convention, the first printed assertion is false: −x2−xy−2y2 also has discriminant −7 but cannot be equivalent to a positive-definite form, because an invertible change of variables preserves its sign.

a OurBigBook.com
The Chebyshev alternation theorem says that a polynomial p of degree at most n is a best uniform approximation to a real continuous function f on a compact interval if and only if there are n+2 ordered points at which f−p attains its uniform norm with alternating signs. For nonzero error these are equal-magnitude alternating extrema; the zero-error case is understood separately. The best approximating polynomial is unique.

b

Words: 100 Articles: 1
2G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 100
b OurBigBook.com
Take xj​=−1+j/4, 0≤j≤8. These nine points satisfy cos(4πxj​)=(−1)j. Thus the zero polynomial has nine alternating error extrema of magnitude one and is minimax among polynomials of degree at most seven by the Chebyshev alternation theorem. Hence every such polynomial has uniform error at least one.
One can also prove the bound directly. If the error were strictly below one everywhere, g(xj​) would have sign (−1)j. The intermediate value theorem would give a distinct zero in each of the eight intervening intervals, contradicting the degree bound. Since the continuous error attains its maximum on the compact interval, there is an x with ∣f(x)−g(x)∣≥1.

3F (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 120
3F OurBigBook.com
For a nonidentity element of PSL2​(R) represented by a determinant-one matrix, the classification is elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic according as the squared trace is less than, equal to or greater than four. This follows either from the eigenvalues or from the discriminant of its fixed-point equation on the boundary of the upper half-plane.
The first matrix has determinant one and trace two, and is not scalar. It is therefore parabolic. Its fixed-point equation is
z=−2z−35z+8​⟺2(z+2)2=0.
(2)
Thus its unique fixed point is z=−2 on the real boundary, of multiplicity two; infinity is not fixed and there is no fixed point in the upper half-plane. The second matrix has determinant one and trace −4, so it is hyperbolic. Its two boundary fixed points are (−1±3​)/2, consistently with this classification.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 154 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 154
4G OurBigBook.com
A decipherable code is one whose extension to finite strings by concatenation is injective: an encoded string has a unique sequence of source letters. In particular its codewords are distinct and nonempty. Put K=∑i​a−si​ and smax​=maxi​si​. For strings of exactly n source letters, let Nj​ count the encoded strings of length j. Unique decipherability gives Nj​≤aj, since distinct source strings yield distinct encoded strings. Expanding Kn gives
Kn=∑j​Nj​a−j≤nsmax​+1.
(3)
Taking nth roots and letting n→∞ proves the McMillan inequality
i∑​a−si​≤1.​
(4)
Add 00,01,10 to the four specified binary words. None of the resulting seven words is a proper suffix of another: the longer words end in 11, and their shorter terminal strings never equal another of the specified longer words. Thus this is a suffix code. Reading from the right determines the last codeword uniquely; deleting it and repeating proves unique decipherability. Its length sum is 3/4+1/8+1/16+2/32=1, in agreement with the bound.

5I (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 122 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 122
5I OurBigBook.com
Independence and the Poisson probabilities give the log-likelihood
ℓ(β)=i=1∑n​(Yi​βxi​−eβxi​−log(Yi​!)).​
(5)
Its score and curvature are
ℓ′(β)=∑i​xi​(Yi​−eβxi​),ℓ′′(β)=−∑i​xi2​eβxi​.
(6)
If some xi​=0, this is strictly concave. A finite maximum is therefore the unique zero of the score when such a zero exists. Newton iteration gives
βm+1​=βm​+∑i​xi2​eβm​xi​∑i​xi​(Yi​−eβm​xi​)​.​
(7)
Start from a finite value, compute the score and curvature, and iterate until both the score and step are small. A line search that shortens a step until the likelihood increases improves robustness. Strict concavity identifies any converged stationary point as the global maximum. A finite root need not exist, for example when all observations are zero and all xi​>0, in which case the likelihood supremum is at β→−∞. If all xi​=0, the parameter is unidentifiable.

6B (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 155 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 155
6B OurBigBook.com
The prey have per-capita growth μ1​, loss through encounters with predators at rate α1​v, and density-dependent competition δu. Predators suffer per-capita mortality μ2​, gain from consuming prey at rate α2​u, and undergo constant harvesting or removal ϵ. Constant harvesting makes the equations biologically valid only while the predator population remains nonnegative.
At an equilibrium with positive populations,
u=δμ1​−α1​v​,v(α2​u−μ2​)=ϵ.
(8)
Writing A=α2​μ1​−δμ2​>0 gives
α1​α2​v2−Av+δϵ=0,v±​=2α1​α2​A±A2−4α1​α2​δϵ​​.​
(9)
For 0<ϵ<A2/(4α1​α2​δ), both roots are positive and give u>μ2​/α2​>0 via the second equilibrium equation. Thus there are two positive equilibria.
Using the equilibrium identities in the Jacobian gives
J=(−δuα2​v​−α1​uϵ/v​),trJ=−δu+vϵ​,detJ=u(α1​α2​v−vδϵ​).​
(10)
The smaller root satisfies v−​v+​=δϵ/(α1​α2​) and v−​<v+​, so v−2​<δϵ/(α1​α2​). Hence its determinant is negative: it is always a saddle and unstable. For small δ,ϵ, this is the equilibrium with u∼μ1​/δ and v∼δϵ/(α2​μ1​), as required. The determinant argument is stronger than merely taking the small-parameter limit.

7E (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 151 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 151
7E OurBigBook.com
A strict Lyapunov function is a continuously differentiable function V with V(0)=0, V(x)>0 off the origin, and ∇V⋅f<0 off the origin in the domain. Its compact sublevel sets inside the domain are forward invariant and force convergence to the equilibrium. The domain of stability, or basin of attraction, consists of initial points whose forward solutions exist for all positive time and converge to the fixed point.
For V=(x2+y2)/2, direct differentiation and factorization give
V˙=−2(x2+y2)+x4+5x2y2+4y4=(x2+y2)(−2+x2+4y2).
(11)
If R2=x2+y2<1/2, then x2+4y2≤4R2<2, so V˙<0 off zero. For any initial point in that disc, choose a slightly larger closed disc still inside it. The vector field points inward on its boundary; the trajectory is bounded, exists globally, and the strict Lyapunov decrease forces its limit to be zero. Thus the origin is asymptotically stable and the whole open disc lies in its basin.
If R2>2, then x2+4y2≥R2>2, so V˙>0. A solution starting there cannot cross inward through R2=2 and cannot approach zero. Therefore
{x2+y2<1/2}⊆B(0)⊆{x2+y2≤2}.​
(12)

8E (Further Complex Methods)

Words: 195 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 195
8E OurBigBook.com
Take a Hankel contour Cη​ around the positive real axis, going from infinity on its lower side toward a circle of radius 0<η<1, clockwise around that circle, then out along the upper side. Use 0≤argz≤2π and define
H(t)=∫Cη​​1+zzte−z​dz.
(13)
This is an entire function of t: the small circle stays away from zero and the pole at −1, while the exponentially decaying rays converge uniformly for t in compact subsets. Contour deformation shows independence of η. For ℜt>−1, let η→0. The upper ray contributes F(t), the lower ray contributes −e2πitF(t), and the small-circle contribution vanishes. Thus the analytic continuation is
F(t)=1−e2πitH(t)​.​
(14)
The only apparent singularities are at integers. At the nonnegative integers they are removable because the original integral is holomorphic throughout ℜt>−1. Hence singularities can occur only at −1,−2,….
In fact all of those points are simple poles. At t=−n−1 the two rays cancel and the clockwise circle gives H(−n−1)=−2πicn​, where
cn​=[zn]1+ze−z​=(−1)n∑j=0n​j!1​=0.
(15)
Since the denominator has derivative −2πi at each integer, the residue at −n−1 is cn​. The parameter has been called t consistently; the final use of z for this parameter in the printed question is harmless notation.

mη¨​1​=−(j+k)η1​+kη2​,mη¨​2​=kη1​−(ℓ+k)η2​.

10D (Cosmology)

Words: 161 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 161
10D OurBigBook.com
An adiabatic change of box size preserves the mode labels, whose momenta scale as p∝L−1. Since V=L3, differentiation gives dp/dV=−p/(3V). Occupation numbers are fixed under this slow mechanical change, so summing the changes in the individual particle energies gives
dE=∫0∞​E′(p)n(p)dp(−3Vp​dV).
(19)
Comparison with dE=−PdV at fixed entropy and particle number yields
P=3V1​∫0∞​pE′(p)n(p)dp.​
(20)
The integration notation means summing over the original momentum-mode labels; it does not assume that the density in momentum space is unchanged after rescaling. In the ultrarelativistic limit E(p)=cp, so pE′(p)=E(p) and P=E/(3V)=ρc2/3.
Adiabatic radiation obeys d(Ea3)=−Pd(a3), giving energy density proportional to a−4. Equilibrium photon energy density is proportional to T4, so T∝a−1. Therefore the photon number in a comoving volume, nγ​a3∝T3a3, is constant. Its entropy is also constant: photon entropy density is (ϵγ​+P)/T∝T3. Photon number is not a microscopic conserved charge, but equilibrium processes maintaining the spectrum do not alter this comoving-number scaling in adiabatic expansion; entropy-producing processes would invalidate the assumptions.

All poles lie outside some circle ∣z∣=R with R>1. The rational function is holomorphic in that disc, so its Taylor series at zero converges uniformly on ∣z∣≤1. Its polynomial partial sums therefore approximate uniformly on K. If there are no finite poles, the function is already a polynomial.

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
Let A be the uniform closure on K of polynomials. It is a closed algebra: uniform convergence on a compact set is preserved under sums and products. For λ∈Λ, put q(z)=(z−λ)−1∈A and d=dist(λ,K)>0. If ∣μ−λ∣<d/2, then μ∈/K and
z−μ1​=∑j=0∞​(μ−λ)jq(z)j+1.
(21)
The series converges uniformly, its ratio having modulus at most one half. Each partial sum is in A, so its limit is too. Hence μ∈Λ in this neighbourhood. For empty K, approximation is vacuous and the assertion is immediate.

12G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 243 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 243
12G OurBigBook.com
A cyclic binary code is a linear subspace of F2n​ invariant under cyclic shifts. Identify a word with its coefficient polynomial in F2​[X]/(Xn−1). Multiplication by X is the shift, so the code is precisely an ideal of that quotient ring. Its inverse image in the polynomial ring is a principal ideal (g) containing (Xn−1); its unique monic generator divides Xn−1. Conversely each monic divisor generates such an ideal. Thus the bijection is with monic divisors; g=1 gives the full code and g=Xn−1 the zero code.
For odd n, some m has n∣2m−1, so the cyclic multiplicative group of F2m​ contains a primitive nth root α. If a nonzero word with the specified roots had weight w<δ, write its nonzero positions as r1​,…,rw​. The root equations give
∑j=1w​cj​(αrj​)i=0(1≤i≤w).
(22)
Their matrix has determinant ∏j​αrj​∏j<l​(αrl​−αrj​)=0, by the Vandermonde formula and distinctness of the positions. Thus all coefficients would vanish, a contradiction. Hence minimum distance is at least δ.
For n=7, choose α with minimal polynomial X3+X+1. The roots α,α2 force also the conjugate α4, giving this cubic as generator. Its degree gives dimension four and its weight gives distance exactly three. Expressing c(α)=0 in a basis of F8​ gives a parity-check matrix with the seven distinct nonzero vectors of F23​ as columns. This is the binary [7,4,3] Hamming code. Its sixteen disjoint radius-one balls have 16(1+7)=128 words, so one-error correction is perfect. The other primitive cubic produces an equivalent coordinate-permuted code.

a OurBigBook.com
T is the interval between generations or censuses, and r the prey multiplication without predators. The factor e−aP can be the probability of escaping a Poisson number of encounters with mean aP, so a measures attack intensity. The factor s converts prey resources into predator recruitment, and b modifies the fraction of prey contributing no recruitment. At b=1 predators recruit from attacked prey; b<1 adds background recruitment, even at P=0. A population interpretation valid at every nonnegative state needs b≤1, since otherwise the second equation gives negative recruitment near P=0.

c OurBigBook.com
The origin has Jacobian (r1−b​00​) and is unstable because r>1. At a positive equilibrium, re−pc​=1, giving
pc​=logr,nc​=r−brlogr​.​
(24)
The linearization is
(pt+1′​nt+1′​​)=(11−b/r​−nc​bnc​/r​)(pt′​nt′​​).
(25)
Its trace is τ=1+bnc​/r and determinant nc​. Elimination gives nt+2′​−τnt+1′​+nc​nt′​=0. For distinct roots,
nt′​=Aλ1t​+Bλ2t​,pt′​=nc​A(1−λ1​)λ1t​+B(1−λ2​)λ2t​​,λ1​+λ2​=τ,λ1​λ2​=nc​.​
(26)
At a repeated root replace the first expression by (A+Bt)λt and use pt′​=(nt′​−nt+1′​)/nc​.
As r↓1, nc​→0, so the roots approach one and zero. The characteristic polynomial at one is nc​(1−b/r)>0, putting the larger real root just below one and the other positive root below it. No real root can ever equal one. Moreover
drdnc​​=(r−b)2r−b−blogr​>0,
(27)
since its numerator exceeds r−1−logr>0. At nc​=1, τ=1+b/r<2, so the roots are conjugate and nonreal. Just above this point their modulus is nc​​>1.
The unit-disc conditions are 1−nc​>0, 1−τ+nc​>0, and 1+τ+nc​>0. The last two hold automatically here, so stability is equivalent to nc​<1. The unique crossing and its eigenvalue argument satisfy
r∗​logr∗​=r∗​−b,1<r∗​<e,2cosθ∗​=1+b/r∗​.​
(28)
Indeed logr∗​=1−b/r∗​<1. This is the stability threshold of a discrete exponential predator-prey model. The sketch uses b=1/2: the real moduli merge and then coincide, increasing through one at the threshold. Linearization decides stability below and instability above; it does not determine nonlinear stability exactly at the crossing.

14E OurBigBook.com
A horseshoe for an interval map consists of an open interval J containing two disjoint open subintervals each mapped onto J. Glendinning chaos means that some positive iterate has a horseshoe.
Solving on the appropriate branches of the tent map gives
x0​=μ+1μ​,x−1​=μ+11​,x−2​=1−μ(μ+1)1​.​
(29)
Here F(x−2​)=x−1​ and F(x−1​)=x0​. On J=[x−1​,x0​] the second iterate is
G(x)={μ−μ2x,μ−μ2+μ2x,​x≤1/2,x≥1/2.​
(30)
Both endpoints map to x0​, and the minimum is v=μ−μ2/2. Both monotone branches cover J when v≤x−1​, equivalently (μ−1)(μ2−2)≥0. Restricting them to preimages of the interior proves a horseshoe for F2 when μ≥2​.
For 1<μ≤2​, G(J)⊆J. Set d=(μ−1)/(μ+1) and h(x)=(x0​−x)/d. This maps J onto [0,1]; substitution in each linear piece gives hGh−1=Fμ2​. The renormalization of the tent map near its fixed point therefore makes F4 conjugate on J to Fμ22​. Applying the preceding threshold proves its horseshoe when 21/4≤μ<2​.
For μ≥2​, the inverse branch of G fixing x0​ contracts distance to x0​ by μ−2. Compose m copies of it with the other inverse branch. This contraction has a fixed point with a periodic itinerary, distinct from x0​ and at distance O(μ−2m). Hence nontrivial periodic points accumulate at x0​.
For μ<2​, the conjugate tent parameter ν=μ2<2 has every nonzero periodic point in [ν−ν2/2,ν/2]. This interval is forward invariant; below it, a nonzero point increases until entering it. The positive lower bound separates those periodic points from zero, which corresponds to x0​. Thus no nontrivial periodic points are sufficiently close to x0​ from the left. A point sufficiently close on the right maps to such a left-hand point; periodicity would pass to its image and is impossible. Thus x0​ is isolated among periodic points, even though a fourth-iterate horseshoe exists elsewhere.

Work with finite graphs, as in the usual matching theorem. Hall's condition is ∣N(A)∣≥∣A∣ for every A⊆X. It is necessary because a matching injects A into its neighbours.
For sufficiency, induct on ∣X∣. If a nonempty proper subset A has ∣N(A)∣=∣A∣, induction matches A to N(A). For B⊆X∖A, Hall's inequality for A∪B gives ∣N(B)∖N(A)∣≥∣B∣, so induction matches the complement to unused neighbours. Combining the matchings finishes this case. Otherwise every nonempty proper A has ∣N(A)∣≥∣A∣+1. Choose an edge xy, delete its endpoints, and observe that every subset of the remaining X still has at least its own number of neighbours. Induction matches the remainder, and adjoining xy finishes. The one-vertex case and the empty case are immediate.
For 0≤d≤∣X∣, the defect version is
G has at least ∣X∣−d independent edges⟺∣N(A)∣≥∣A∣−d for all A⊆X.​
(35)
Necessity follows because at most d vertices of X can be unmatched. For sufficiency add d new vertices to Y, each joined to every vertex of X. The displayed inequality makes Hall's condition hold in the enlarged graph. Its full matching uses at most d new vertices, giving the required original edges.
To prove the matching-cover equality, let M be a maximum matching and U its unmatched vertices in X. Follow alternating paths from U, using nonmatching edges from X to Y and matching edges back. Let ZX​,ZY​ be the reachable sets. No reachable Y is unmatched, since that would give an augmenting path and a larger matching. Matching edges give a bijection ZY​↔ZX​∖U. The set C=(X∖ZX​)∪ZY​ covers every edge: an edge from a reachable X to an unreachable Y cannot be a nonmatching edge, and its matching edge, if present, is already reachable. Its size is
∣C∣=∣X∣−∣ZX​∣+∣ZY​∣=∣X∣−∣U∣=∣M∣.
(36)
Every vertex cover has at least ∣M∣ vertices, because the matching edges are disjoint. Therefore maximum matching size equals minimum vertex-cover size, as required.

18H (Galois Theory)

Words: 402 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 402
18H OurBigBook.com
Begin with two points at distance one. A ruler draws the line through two known points; a compass draws a circle with a known centre and a constructible radius. New points are intersections of such lines and circles. A real number is constructible when it occurs as a coordinate of a point obtained by finitely many such operations; a complex point is constructible when both coordinates are.
If current coordinates lie in a field K⊆R, a line-line intersection solves linear equations over K, while line-circle or circle-circle intersections reduce to a quadratic equation over K. Thus each step requires at most adjoining a square root. Consequently every constructible number lies in a tower
Q=K0​⊆K1​⊆⋯⊆Km​,[Ki+1​:Ki​]≤2.
(37)
Conversely field sums and differences are obtained by laying off segments, products and quotients by similar triangles, and a positive square root by the geometric-mean construction in a semicircle. Hence every real number in such a tower is constructible. This proves the quadratic-tower criterion, not merely its necessity.
In particular a constructible algebraic number has degree a power of two. Degree alone is not sufficient in general; the exact criterion is containment in a quadratic tower. Equivalently the Galois group of its normal closure is a finite two-group: a tower's normal closure remains a two-extension, and a two-group admits a chain of subgroups with successive index two, yielding the converse by Galois correspondence.
The standard impossibility results follow. Doubling a unit-volume cube requires 32​, whose polynomial X3−2 is irreducible by Eisenstein and has degree three. Trisecting an arbitrary angle would in particular trisect 60 degrees, requiring 2cos20∘, a root of X3−3X−1. This cubic has no rational root and is irreducible, so this construction is impossible, although some particular angles can be trisected. Squaring the unit circle requires side length π​, impossible because π is transcendental whereas constructible numbers are algebraic.
For a regular n-gon, constructibility is equivalent to that of e2πi/n. The cyclotomic extension is Galois of degree φ(n), so it is constructible exactly when this degree is a power of two. Writing the prime factorization of n shows the equivalent condition
n=2ap1​⋯ps​,pi​ distinct Fermat primes.​
(38)
Indeed odd prime exponents must be one, and each pi​−1 must be a power of two. If 2m+1 is prime, m must itself be a power of two by factoring when m has an odd divisor. Conversely this factorization makes the cyclotomic Galois group a two-group and provides a quadratic tower. This gives both positive constructions, such as the regular seventeen-gon, and obstructions, such as the regular seven-gon.

The Simplicial approximation theorem states that a continuous map between realizations of finite simplicial complexes becomes homotopic to a simplicial map after sufficiently many barycentric subdivisions of the domain. More precisely, a vertex assignment is a simplicial approximation when the image of each open star is contained in the open star of its assigned vertex; sufficiently fine subdivision permits such an assignment. The resulting straight-line homotopy stays in the appropriate target simplices.
The vertices of a barycentric subdivision are the barycentres of nonempty faces. An n-simplex has 2n+1−1 such faces. A top-dimensional subdivided simplex corresponds to a full flag of faces of sizes 1,2,…,n+1, equivalently to an ordering of the original vertices. Thus
#vertices=2n+1−1,#top-dimensional simplices=(n+1)!.​
(43)
Triangulate both copies of the sphere using finite complexes. For each fixed subdivision level there are only finitely many vertex maps to the finite target vertex set, hence only finitely many simplicial maps. Every continuous map is homotopic to one of them at some finite level. A countable union of finite sets is countable, proving at most countably many homotopy classes without needing their classification by degree.

A subset is nowhere dense when its closure has empty interior. It is of first category, or meagre, when it is a countable union of nowhere-dense subsets; otherwise it is of second category.
The Baire category theorem says that in a complete metric space every countable intersection of open dense subsets is dense. To prove it, start inside an arbitrary nonempty open set and choose a closed ball of positive radius there and in the first dense open set. Inductively choose a closed ball inside the interior of the preceding ball and the next dense open set, with radius less than 2−n. The centres are Cauchy. Completeness gives a limit lying in all the nested closed balls, hence in all the dense open sets and the original open set. Thus a nonempty complete metric space is not meagre in itself.
For p<r≤∞, put Em​={x∈ℓp:∥x∥p​≤m}, viewed inside ℓr. Necessarily p<∞. Each Em​ is closed: convergence in the ℓr norm gives coordinatewise convergence, and every finite partial sum of ∑∣xi​∣p is bounded by mp in the limit. Taking the supremum of partial sums proves the assertion.
It has empty interior. Given a point in it and any small ℓr radius, perturb a block of N coordinates by entries of modulus δN−1/r, choosing signs to avoid cancelling the existing coordinates. The ℓr distance is δ, while the resulting ℓp norm is at least δN1/p−1/r, exceeding m for large N. For r=∞, use entries of modulus δ on that block. Hence each Em​ is nowhere dense, and
ℓp=m=1⋃∞​Em​ is first category in ℓr (p<r).​
(44)
For r=p, including p=∞, the space is Banach and so second category in itself by Baire. There is no case r>p when p=∞.

A Riemann surface is a Hausdorff, second-countable, one-dimensional complex manifold, with charts to open subsets of C whose transition maps are holomorphic. Connectedness is often included in the convention. A map between Riemann surfaces is holomorphic when its expression in every compatible pair of charts is holomorphic. It is biholomorphic when it is bijective and both it and its inverse are holomorphic.

Choose a common target chart and a source disc around p on which both images lie in that chart. Their coordinate difference is holomorphic and vanishes at accumulating points from A, so the identity theorem makes it vanish on the disc. Thus p∈A. Therefore A is also closed, and connectedness implies f=g on all of R.

One complete cycle consists of ten stops of mean one minute and ten journeys of mean four minutes, so its mean duration is fifty minutes. Over the eight-hour shift, the elementary renewal approximation gives 480/50=9.6 completed circuits on average.
For the end-of-shift calculation use the long-run occupation probabilities of the twenty successive phases. Each stop phase has probability 1/50, and each travel phase probability 4/50. Alighting stop j is therefore selected with probability 1/50+4/50=1/10, from either stopping there or travelling toward it. If that stop is the station, no further stops are passed. If it is stop j≥2, the intermediate stops are j+1,…,10, numbering 10−j. Thus the requested approximate mean is
101​(0+8+7+⋯+1+0)=3.6.​
(51)
The approximation treats eight hours as long compared with a cycle and ignores the initial-phase transient. Exponential holding times justify the twenty-phase Markov description; independent cycle times justify the renewal rate.

A statistic is sufficient when the conditional distribution of the observation given it does not depend on the parameter. It is minimal sufficient when it is, up to null sets, a measurable function of every sufficient statistic. For a dominated family, the likelihood-ratio criterion identifies two observations precisely when their likelihood ratio is independent of the parameter.
The Rao–Blackwell theorem says that conditioning a square-integrable unbiased estimator on a sufficient statistic preserves unbiasedness and cannot increase variance. The Cramér–Rao bound for an unbiased estimator of scalar θ is Varθ​θ≥1/I(θ). It requires parameter-independent support, differentiability, interchange of differentiation and integration, and finite positive Fisher information. More generally the numerator is the square of the derivative of the estimand. The bound follows from Eθ​[θ∂θ​logf]=1 and Cauchy–Schwarz.
For the uniform sample, the joint likelihood is θ−n1{0<xi​<θ ∀i}​. Its dependence on the observations is through T=maxi​Xi​, proving sufficiency. Two such likelihoods have parameter-independent ratio exactly when their maxima coincide, proving minimality. The density of T is ntn−1/θn on (0,θ). Unbiasedness of h(T) says
∫0θ​nh(t)tn−1dt=θn+1.

Differentiating this absolutely continuous identity gives h(t)=(n+1)t/n almost everywhere. Conversely that function is unbiased. Under any competing policy, iterate its Bellman inequality to obtain V(x)≥E[∑t=0N−1​βtr(xt​,ut​)+βNV(xN​)]. Drop the nonnegative terminal term and let N→∞. Monotone convergence gives V(x)≥F(π,x) for every competitor. Since V is the actual return of π, this proves optimality without a transversality assumption.
Assume the income process remains nonnegative, as required by the feasible-control interval; for unrestricted feasible controls a sufficient condition is ϵt​≥−1. If β≤1/(1+θ)<1, spending everything gives constant income x and value V(x)=x/(1−β). Its Bellman expression for general u is
u+1−ββ​{x+θ(x−u)}=1−ββ(1+θ)x+[1−β(1+θ)]u​.
(57)
The coefficient of u is nonnegative, so the maximum over [0,x] occurs at u=x and equals V(x). Therefore spending all income at every step is optimal.
If 1/(1+θ)<β<1 and x>0, invest all income for T steps and thereafter spend everything. Its expected return is x[β(1+θ)]T/(1−β), unbounded as T→∞. In fact a sufficiently small fixed positive consumption fraction gives infinite expected discounted reward if β[1+θ(1−c)]≥1. Thus the value is infinite and the problem has no finite-valued optimum. For β=1, spending everything already gives infinite value when x>0. If x=0, the value is zero. A mean condition alone, without nonnegative income or equivalent admissibility restrictions, would not make the model well-defined.

A fundamental solution of a constant-coefficient operator P(D) is a distribution E satisfying P(D)E=δ0​. The proposed N is locally integrable in three dimensions and harmonic away from zero. For a smooth compactly supported test function φ, apply Green's identity outside the ball of radius η. On the inner boundary the outward normal is −r^, so ∂ν​N=1/(4πη2). The outer boundary contributes nothing. Thus
∫∣x∣>η​N(−Δφ)dx=∫∣x∣=η​(4πη2φ​+4πη∂r​φ​)dS.
(58)
The first term tends to φ(0) and the second is O(η). Local integrability permits taking the limit on the left. Therefore −ΔN=δ0​ in distributions.
For a harmonic function on a ball, define its spherical mean M(r)=(4π)−1∫S2​u(x0​+rω)dω. Differentiation and the divergence theorem give M′(r)=(4πr2)−1∫Br​(x0​)​Δu=0. Its limit at zero is u(x0​), so
u(x0​)=4πr21​∫∂Br​(x0​)​udS=∣Br​∣1​∫Br​(x0​)​udx.​
(59)
The ball formula follows by integrating spherical means in the radius. If two solutions of the prescribed Poisson equation tend to zero at infinity, their difference is globally harmonic and also tends to zero. Apply the spherical mean at an arbitrary x0​ and let r→∞; every point of that sphere has distance at least r−∣x0​∣ from the origin, so the mean tends to zero. Hence the difference is zero everywhere, proving uniqueness.

Orient the circle counterclockwise and define its Cauchy transform
Φ(z)=2πi1​∫C​τ−zϕ(τ)​dτ.
(60)
The inside and outside limits satisfy Φ+​−Φ−​=ϕ and Φ+​+Φ−​=(πi)−1PV∫C​ϕ(τ)/(τ−t)dτ. Also Φ−​(z)=O(z−1) at infinity. Applying these formulas to the two polynomial coefficients and dividing by t2 gives the Riemann–Hilbert condition
(t2−1)Φ+​(t)−tΦ−​(t)=(A−1)t+1.​
(61)
The homogeneous jump is G=t/(t2−1). A canonical factorization of a rational scalar Riemann-Hilbert jump is
X+​(z)=1,X−​(z)=z−z−1,G=X+​/X−​.​
(62)
The inside factor is analytic and nonvanishing; the exterior factor has no zeros or poles outside the circle and grows like z. The jump index is 1−2=−1, consistently with this growth.
Put F+​=Φ+​ and F−​=Φ−​/X−​. Their additive jump is R(t)=((A−1)t+1)/(t2−1). Since R is analytic outside the circle and decays there, the functions F+​ inside and F−​+R outside glue to an entire function. This function tends to zero at infinity, so Liouville's theorem gives F+​=0, F−​=−R. Consequently
Φ+​=0,Φ−​=−z(A−1)z+1​.
(63)
The required decay of a Cauchy transform forces A=1. Then Φ−​=−1/z, and the jump gives
ϕ(t)=1/t.​
(64)
For the homogeneous problem, Φ+​/X+​ and Φ−​/X−​ glue to an entire function vanishing at infinity, so only the zero solution exists; this proves uniqueness. Direct verification uses the principal-value integral −πi/t: the two terms on the left combine to (t4+t3−t2−t4+t3+t2)/(2t)=t2, exactly the right side at A=1.

The one-particle transformation is the matrix R=(cs​−sc​), with determinant one. The antisymmetric tensor ∣↑↓⟩−∣↓↑⟩ transforms by this determinant under R⊗R, so the singlet is unchanged. The total Sz​ kills it. Its invariance under these rotations implies that total Sz​cosθ+Sx​sinθ also kills it for every θ, so total Sx​ kills it. The spin commutator then gives total Sy​ acting as zero. Therefore S2∣χ⟩=0 and it has total spin zero.
Rotating only particle B produces
∣χθ​⟩=2​1​(−s∣↑↑⟩+c∣↑↓⟩−c∣↓↑⟩−s∣↓↓⟩).

Each arrow represents the corresponding value ±ℏ/2. The sequential measurements commute because they act on different particles. The two parallel outcomes leave triplet states with total spin one and S2=2ℏ2. Each antiparallel product state is a superposition of the spin-zero singlet and the spin-one zero-projection triplet, and is not an S2 eigenstate. Outcomes of zero probability at a special angle do not actually occur.

For a periodic potential, the Hamiltonian commutes with every lattice translation. The three primitive translations are commuting unitary operators, so within each energy eigenspace one can choose simultaneous translation eigenstates. Their eigenvalues have modulus one and can be written eik⋅ai​. Translation by any lattice vector then gives
ψnk​(r+l)=eik⋅lψnk​(r),ψnk​=eik⋅runk​(r),u(r+l)=u(r).​
(67)
This proves Bloch's theorem in its eigenbasis form; arbitrary superpositions inside a degenerate eigenspace need not themselves have a single Bloch wavevector.
The reciprocal lattice consists of vectors g with g⋅ai​∈2πZ. Changing k to k+g and u to e−ig⋅ru gives the same physical wavefunction with a periodic new u. The eigenvalue problem on one cell has a discrete set of levels, giving bands indexed by n, and this equivalence yields En​(k+g)=En​(k). A reciprocal-lattice fundamental domain, conventionally a Brillouin zone, therefore labels inequivalent wavevectors.
Periodic boundary conditions in physical volume V give one allowed wavevector per reciprocal-space volume (2π)3/V. Including the two spin states, there are 2Vd3k/(2π)3 states; per unit physical volume the count is the printed 2d3k/(2π)3. Each occupied state carries charge −e and velocity ℏ−1∇k​En​, so
j=−e(2π)32​∫B​n(k)v(k)d3k.​
(68)
For a full band, the integral of ∇k​En​ is a boundary integral. Opposite faces of a reciprocal fundamental cell have equal energies by periodicity and opposite normals, so their contributions cancel. Hence a full band carries zero electric current.

(∂V∂CV​​)T​=T(∂T2∂2P​)V​.​

In the lubrication regime the thin region has longitudinal scale ℓ∼ab​, since the height increase x2/(2a) becomes comparable with b there. The characteristic shear is μV/b, so force per axial length scales as μVℓ/b∼μVa/b​. Negligible inertia, no slip, no cylinder rotation, and full wetting are understood.
Use a frame translating with the cylinder. The wall moves with velocity −V, the cylinder is stationary, and the gap is h(x)=b+x2/(2a). Lubrication momentum gives μuyy​=px​, py​=0, so
uframe​=−V(1−y/h)+2μpx​​y(y−h),q=−2Vh​−12μh3px​​.
(76)
Continuity makes q constant. Equal ambient pressures at both infinities give ∫px​dx=0, hence q=−(V/2)(∫h−2dx)/(∫h−3dx)=−2Vb/3. Therefore
px​=h32μV(4b−3h)​,p=h22μVx​,ulab​=hVy​+2μpx​​y(y−h).​

The vertical velocity, with the wall condition w(0)=0, follows explicitly from incompressibility:
w=2h2Vh′y2​−2μpxx​​(3y3​−2hy2​)+4μpx​h′y2​.
(78)
It gives w(h)=0, consistently with a horizontally translating cylinder in the lab frame.
The wall shear is μuy​(0)=4μV(1/h−b/h2). With x=2ab​s, its integral is
F=4μV2ab​(bπ​−2bπ​),F∼2πμVb2a​​(b/a→0).​
(79)
Force balance equates this wall force to the required cylinder force at leading order; the pressure and viscous stresses on remote boundaries make no leading contribution. This is the cylinder translating parallel to a wall in a thin gap result. The asymptotic sign denotes the approximation implicit in the parabolic gap, rather than an exact finite-gap cylinder formula.

Assume the consistency regularity implicit in the requested rate, for example u∈C4 on the closed square. Bounded fourth derivatives and Taylor's theorem give a uniform residual τij​=Δh​u(ih,jh)−f(ih,jh) with ∣τij​∣≤C0​h2. Subtracting the exact grid values from the numerical equations gives Δh​e=−τ, with zero boundary error.
Let A=−h2Δh​ be the unscaled positive Dirichlet matrix. Its eigenvectors are products of discrete sine vectors, which form an orthogonal basis; direct substitution gives eigenvalues
λpq​=4sin22pπh​+4sin22qπh​(1≤p,q≤M).
(83)
Since sin(πh/2)≥h for 0<h≤1, λ11​≥8h2. Therefore ∥A−1∥2​≤1/(8h2). The error equation is Ae=h2τ, and its residual has norm ∥τ∥2​≤MC0​h2≤C0​h. Combining the bounds yields
(i,j=1∑M​∣eij​∣2)1/2≤8C0​​h.​
(84)
This is the unweighted grid error for the five-point Poisson formula. The unweighted norm loses one power of h because the grid has order h−2 points; the area-weighted norm is second-order accurate. A regularity assumption is needed for the uniform truncation estimate and hence for this rate; the question does not specify it explicitly.
